summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia stands under the national framework: since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice". Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, national identification documents carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025, and a comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025. The courts have also ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report, "Un sistema que falla: prejuicio, violencia e impunidad contra personas LGBTIQ+ en Colombia", finds that one LGBTIQ+ person was killed every 32 hours during 2025, and that violence escalates along a continuum from discrimination to intrafamily violence (1,531 cases), sexual violence (628 cases), threats (1,184 victims), homicide and impunity. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

The counts that describe this violence cannot be reconciled between sources. El Tiempo's 2025 data investigation reports that the Fiscalía's own database records 3,322 intentional homicides of people identified as LGBTIQ+ between January 2010 and May 2025, including 431 for 2024 against roughly 600 fewer reported by the NGO figure of about 160, and 39 homicides in one Fiscalía dependency's 2025 data against 156 in the policies-and-strategies base. Experts cited in the investigation describe the information system as neither unified nor reliable.

Caribe Afirmativo documents territorial expansion of this violence toward territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence, together with insufficient state response. The report does not name Bolívar explicitly; the department nevertheless sits within the cluster flagged for that expansion and weakest response, and the killing in Carmen de Bolívar is covered by the El Tiempo investigation.

Bolívar's specific signal is a named, targeted killing. Nawar Jiménez, a trans social leader who had campaigned with the 'No Es Hora De Callar' movement and joined its sixth symbolic return march of more than 500 survivors of sexual violence, was killed in Carmen de Bolívar on 22 May 2025; the El Tiempo article characterises it as a trans feminicide. More than 19 days later the circumstances of what happened remained unclear, and her friend and fellow social leader Yirley Velasco remembers her as having taken up the fight for trans rights in the municipality.

Versus the national score of approximately 0.52, Bolívar sits about 0.08 lower, a gap resting on this single documented high-profile homicide rather than on any wider enforcement finding for the department.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's pattern of targeted killings of trans people is not confined to territories where armed groups hold sway. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault circulated from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, solidarity events were held in several cities, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control, the violence is announced in advance. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns publicised through flyers targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" and threatened a further wave; trans women there reported few options beyond sex work, trans salon owner Tatiana Cespedes was forced to relocate twice after death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
localsOnly:
For residents of Bolívar, as for all Colombians, the sex marker on government identification is changed by signing a document before a notary, a route available since June 2015, and legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition recognised in Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 with no surgical requirement. Identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025.

Marriage equality has been available nationally since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015. Rights of trans detainees in the prison system have been the subject of a court ruling on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty. A comprehensive trans law remained before the legislature in 2025, so residents live under the existing mix of constitutional jurisprudence, statutory provisions and administrative rules rather than under a single consolidated statute.

Residents also face the enforcement picture documented above: a homicide count for LGBTIQ+ people that official and NGO databases state differently, and a monitoring organisation reporting an LGBTIQ+ person killed every 32 hours nationally in 2025. The 22 May 2025 killing of Nawar Jiménez in Carmen de Bolívar was, at more than 19 days, still without a clear account of what happened.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bolívar departmental statute, municipal ordinance, enforcement practice, or official facility ruling specific to trans people is sourced in this inventory; the departmental signal rests on a single documented homicide. Whether further unreported incidents occurred in Bolívar during 2025 is unresolved and not sourced here.

Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 report does not name Bolívar; the department's placement within the flagged cluster of territories with illegal-economy corridors and weak state presence is an inference from the report's stated pattern, not an express finding about Bolívar, and the report's own counts are not itemised by department.

The discrepancy between official and civil-society homicide totals is itself unresolved in the sources: the Fiscalía database figures (3,322 from January 2010 to May 2025; 431 in 2024; 39 in one 2025 dependency) and the NGO figures (about 160 for 2024; 156 in the policies-and-strategies base) are not reconciled, and the experts cited call the information system neither unified nor reliable. The same caution applies to the separate national count of 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025 attributed to the Attorney General's Office.

Whether the killing of Nawar Jiménez has since been investigated, whether suspects have been identified or charged, and whether the circumstances became clear after the 19-day window reported are not sourced. The approximately 0.08 shortfall against the national score of about 0.52 is not derived from any departmental enforcement dataset in this inventory.
